analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal fuel economy requirements for new cars and trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal corporate average fuel economy standards never left committee — no hearing, no vote — and died when the Congress ended, leaving the standards in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards, the federal rules requiring carmakers to make their fleets travel a set distance per gallon of fuel [S2] [S3]. Repeal would free automakers from those requirements, letting them sell more gas-hungry vehicles, but drivers would spend more on gasoline and more fuel would be burned overall [S2]. The bill was introduced by Rep. Scott Perry with three cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers are the main beneficiaries: repeal would end the requirement that their fleets meet average fuel economy levels, eliminating the compliance costs and fines tied to selling less efficient vehicles [S2] [S3]. Oil companies would also gain, since a vehicle fleet that travels fewer miles per gallon burns more gasoline. Some buyers of large trucks and SUVs might see lower upfront sticker prices, though they would pay for it at the pump over the life of the vehicle.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Chapter 329 of title 49, U.S. Code — the corporate average fuel economy standards — in its entirety, removing the legal mandate that automakers' new-vehicle fleets meet average miles-per-gallon levels [S3].

With the standards gone, automakers would no longer face compliance costs, credit purchases, or penalties tied to fleet fuel economy, freeing them to build and sell whatever mix of vehicles is cheapest for them to produce [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Drivers would pay more at the gas pump, since the standards are what push cars and trucks to travel farther on a gallon of fuel [S2]. Households would also bear the health and environmental costs of burning more gasoline, and the U.S. vehicle fleet would consume more oil overall.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the main federal force pushing vehicles to use less fuel, so drivers would spend more on gasoline every year — the exact cost the standards exist to hold down [S2].
Burning more gasoline means more tailpipe emissions and oil consumption, costs that fall on the public rather than on the manufacturers freed from the rules [S2].

Repealing the standards outright, rather than adjusting them, would also remove the certainty automakers use to plan multi-year vehicle designs, and could leave U.S. cars less competitive on fuel costs against vehicles built to stricter standards elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to automakers in the form of avoided compliance costs, while the costs — higher gasoline spending for every household that drives, plus more oil consumption and emissions — land on the public [S2]. The savings to buyers at the dealership would be outweighed over a vehicle's life by the extra fuel it burns. The bill offered no offsetting consumer protection or alternative efficiency policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sat there for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on April 20, 2023, with Reps. Tiffany and Ogles as original cosponsors; it would repeal the fuel economy standards in Chapter 329 of title 49, U.S. Code [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce — the only committee action it ever received [S1] [S5].

It attracted just 4 cosponsors, all Republicans, out of 224 House Republicans, and never advanced to a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the fuel economy standards stayed in place, so drivers keep the fleet-efficiency rules that hold down gasoline spending, and the oil and auto interests that wanted repeal got nothing.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the fuel economy standards

for.name: 4 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Tiffany and Ogles as original cosponsors

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 5 of 224 House Republicans signed on — no Democrat supported it, and the bill never reached a vote where the split could be recorded.

industries.note: Repeal would lift the fleet fuel economy requirements that force automakers to sell more efficient vehicles, cutting their compliance costs [S2]. The saving comes at drivers' expense through higher gasoline use over each vehicle's life.
A fleet that travels fewer miles per gallon burns more fuel, so repeal would raise gasoline demand — the opposite of what the standards achieve [S2].
Households would pay more for fuel each year and bear the added pollution burden; this is the population the standards were written to protect [S2].
